Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/

articles.title: One UWB Radar, Many Views: Comparing and Fusing Signal Representations for Human Activity Recognition
articles.summary: IEEE 802.15.4z-compliant impulse-radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) transceivers are increasingly built into consumer devices, enabling contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR) in…
articles.abstract: IEEE 802.15.4z-compliant impulse-radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB) transceivers are increasingly built into consumer devices, enabling contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR) in healthcare. Before activity classification, the signal is typically converted into range-time, range-Doppler, or time-Doppler maps, each exposing different spatial and motion cues. Existing comparisons often apply shared processing across representations, leaving it unclear whether their rankings hold after independent tuning. It is also unknown whether rankings and fusion gains generalize across environments and activities, and at what computational cost. Consequently, practitioners lack guidance on which representation and processing suit a given HAR deployment. We release an open dataset of raw IR-UWB measurements collected by a ceiling-mounted radar from 44 participants during scripted activity sequences in 12 layouts across two bedrooms. Using a statistically guided, staged search, we independently tune each representation across five processing and deployment settings. We then compare individual and fused performance under layout and room shifts and quantify computational cost. Across over 1{,}000 cross-validated models, independent tuning proves essential, as optimal processing differs per representation and processing choices shift macro-F1 by up to 26 points, four times the gap between representations. Once tuned, the range-Doppler map leads for unseen layouts (85.1\% macro-F1), while time-Doppler map does for unseen rooms (72.7\%). Fusing all three maps raises these scores to 89.1\% and 80.0\%, respectively. Lower sampling rates and narrower Doppler bands reduce latency by 38--51\% with at most a 1.5-point macro-F1 loss. The best representation for UWB HAR is therefore a deployment decision, not a fixed property.

articles.title: Automated Neural Network Auditing (ANNA) for Energy Market Settlements: A Machine and Reinforcement Learning-Based Approach
articles.summary: The integration of segmented energy markets into Independent System Operators (ISOs) like CAISO and MISO has increased settlement complexity. Automated transaction processing creates challenges for…
articles.abstract: The integration of segmented energy markets into Independent System Operators (ISOs) like CAISO and MISO has increased settlement complexity. Automated transaction processing creates challenges for evaluating accuracy, compliance, and financial integrity. Traditional rule-based manual auditing is inefficient, error-prone, and cannot handle the data volume from automated markets.This research proposes Automated Neural Network Auditing (ANNA), a machine and reinforcement learning framework for settlement auditing via anomaly prioritization. ANNA integrates statistical anomaly detection, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), clustering, and Deep Q-Network (DQN) reinforcement learning to flag potentially anomalous transactions from historical market data. The approach is evaluated as an analyst-support tool for prioritizing transactions needing further audit review.ANNA was tested against traditional statistical methods, clustering-based techniques, and supervised/reinforcement learning models. The study used three years of CAISO settlement data over 63 million source records across 32 charge codes and multiple counterparties. After preprocessing, approximately 2.9 million labeled transactions formed the working dataset, with model-specific subsets used for training and evaluation. Performance was assessed using precision, recall, computational efficiency, and false-negative detection.ANNA outperforms traditional methods by identifying hidden relationships in settlement data, while standard deviation thresholds, K-Means, KNN, and Q-Learning performed poorly across key metrics. The result is a scalable solution integrating machine and reinforcement learning for automated auditing of energy market settlements, contributing computationally efficient anomaly prioritization to settlement-auditing workflows.

articles.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
articles.summary: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and…
articles.abstract: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

articles.title: Antiphony: A Dual-Process Agent for Deepfake Video Detection with Real-Video Calibration
articles.summary: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may…
articles.abstract: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.

articles.title: Categorical Foundations of AI Agents
articles.summary: We follow the idea of separating intelligence from execution and give the categorical foundations of AI agents: the transformers, the agents, and the orchestrations and choreographies of AI agents…
articles.abstract: We follow the idea of separating intelligence from execution and give the categorical foundations of AI agents: the transformers, the agents, and the orchestrations and choreographies of AI agents are categorized, and which also include their coalgebras and algebras.

articles.title: Differential Proteomics to XAI Rules: A SHAP-FOL-ILP Modeling for Lung Adenocarcinoma
articles.summary: Background: We developed an interpretable workflow linking paired differential proteomics, sparse logistic regression, SHAP attribution, and first-order logic (FOL) rule learning in lung…
articles.abstract: Background: We developed an interpretable workflow linking paired differential proteomics, sparse logistic regression, SHAP attribution, and first-order logic (FOL) rule learning in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). Methods: We analysed 213 CPTAC-LUAD tissue samples (111 tumour, 102 adjacent-normal) from 111 patients, including 102 matched pairs. Protein effect estimation and testing used the same complete pairs, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Sparse logistic regression used five-fold stratified patient-grouped nested cross-validation. Preprocessing and model selection were confined to training data, with feature selection repeated within inner folds. A separate five-fold patient-grouped evaluation tested SHAP-guided inductive logic programming (FOL/ILP) using training-derived evidence and discretisation. Results: Quality control retained 9,518 proteins. At FDR below 0.05 and an absolute mean paired log-ratio difference of at least 1, 378 were differentially abundant (40 increased, 338 decreased). The sparse classifier yielded ROC-AUC 0.9997, average precision 0.9998, accuracy 0.9906, and balanced accuracy 0.9906. FOL/ILP yielded held-out accuracy 0.9765, balanced accuracy 0.9767, precision 0.9818, recall 0.9730, and F1 0.9774. HSPA12B, PALM2-AKAP2, STARD13, and PPM1F had non-zero coefficients in all five classifier folds. The most frequent Horn clause occurred in two of five folds. All others occurred once. Conclusions: The workflow connects proteomic classification, attribution, and symbolic rules. Performance reflects tumour-versus-adjacent-normal discrimination within one cohort. Biomarker and clinical claims require independent validation, repeated assessment of rule stability, and further biological annotation.

articles.title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current
articles.summary: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue…
articles.abstract: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.

articles.title: Separating Genetic and Protein Evidence in Open Targets: An Auditable Re-ranking Study
articles.summary: Biomedical target-ranking platforms combine genetics, literature, experimental evidence, tractability, and clinical precedent because each is useful for target discovery. A single integrated score,…
articles.abstract: Biomedical target-ranking platforms combine genetics, literature, experimental evidence, tractability, and clinical precedent because each is useful for target discovery. A single integrated score, however, can be awkward to reuse for a narrower question such as which genes have direct evidence for disease risk or etiology. We examine this issue in Open Targets associations for Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson disease (PD). Genetics-linked evidence and protein-oriented evidence are scored in separate channels and combined only at the end. In AD, the Open Targets overall top 20 contains 7 curated genetics-supported genes and 10 symptomatic pharmacology controls; the default late fusion contains 15 curated genes and no symptomatic controls. In PD, late fusion retains 13 curated genes and removes the 5 symptomatic controls present in the platform top 20. A genetics-only ranking reaches similar curated recall (14 genes in AD, 13 in PD), so most of the gain over the platform score comes from emphasizing genetic evidence; the protein channel mainly raises the number of tractable targets in the shortlist (from 9 to 12 in AD and from 8 to 10 in PD) without readmitting symptomatic controls. These results are stable across fusion weights from 0.35 to 0.75, perturbed protein-channel weights, and rule thresholds. An optional post-ranking rule further lowers high-clinical/low-genetic targets such as ACHE and GRIN1 without changing top-20 curated recall. The procedure is deterministic and uses public Open Targets fields. Because the component scores remain available, individual rank changes can be inspected and the ranking can be reproduced from the same data snapshot.

articles.title: Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection
articles.summary: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain…
articles.abstract: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.

articles.title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters
articles.summary: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a…
articles.abstract: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated. We examine several methods for reducing inconsistency, including prompting, consistency training using GRPO, and iterative rule refinement. As in human statutory interpretation, surrounding rules shape how a rule is interpreted. Unlike the legal setting, however, these interactions are currently happening implicitly inside the judge model's reasoning. We argue that multi-rule interactions must be measured and handled explicitly by ruleset designers to prevent undetected shifts in interpretation from causing downstream alignment failures.

articles.title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
articles.summary: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces,…
articles.abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D}{CARE-3D}.

articles.title: When Learned IDS Model Selection Collapses to a Static Choice: A Measurement Study at the Edge
articles.summary: Runtime model selection trades detection quality against energy and latency. However, comparing a selector only with a more costly static detector conflates detector choice with the benefit of…
articles.abstract: Runtime model selection trades detection quality against energy and latency. However, comparing a selector only with a more costly static detector conflates detector choice with the benefit of adaptation. We present a framework for analysis and physical measurement that combines a pairwise reward criterion, matched static controls, paired blocks, a fixed load-prevalence factorial design, and reporting of actions outside training support. On one Raspberry Pi 4B with four frozen TON-IoT detectors, tabular Q-learning and a deep Q-network (DQN) both select LightLR throughout. A retrospective audit using validation data only rules out preference reversals for MedRF versus LightLR and HeavyMLP versus LightLR. However, TinyDT has a higher reward than LightLR in seven of the 2,500 windows, so the audit does not establish global LightLR optimality. We also evaluate a causal DeadlineGuard rule under a fixed factorial design with three arrival rates (50, 100, and 4,000 rows/s) and three attack prevalences (0.10, 0.50, and 0.90). Compared with Static-MedRF, DeadlineGuard saves 43.7 J per 500-s run (2.98%; 95% paired CI 41.4--46.0 J) and eliminates all 512 deadline misses among 5,000 windows, at a cost of 1.373 percentage points in F1. Outside training support, Tabular-Q's deterministic tie-breaking rule selects TinyDT, resulting in a false-positive rate of 67.76%. These single-board results motivate joint audits of reward attainability, realized actions, attribution against matched static controls, service feasibility, and default actions outside training support.

articles.title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
articles.summary: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual…
articles.abstract: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

articles.title: Reward Blindness: A Theoretical Framework for Diagnosing Reinforcement Learning Reward Limitations in Text-to-SQL
articles.summary: Text-to-SQL systems let users without programming expertise query relational databases in natural language. Reinforcement learning has become the dominant way to train such systems, yet progress is…
articles.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems let users without programming expertise query relational databases in natural language. Reinforcement learning has become the dominant way to train such systems, yet progress is still judged by a single number, execution accuracy, which counts correct queries but says nothing about which kinds of semantic error survive training. This paper develops a theoretical framework that examines text-to-SQL from the perspective of reward design. We introduce Reward Error Sensitivity, a measure of how strongly a reward function separates queries that contain a given error type from queries that do not, and prove a Reward Blindness theorem: when this sensitivity is zero, policy-gradient training carries no systematic signal for removing that error. Using fourteen published finegrained error signals for four text-to-SQL systems on the BIRD benchmark, we build error profiles and estimate sensitivities for common reward designs. Predicate and result-level errors are the most frequent, firing on up to 27 percent of queries, while structurally deep errors such as suboptimal joins persist at 5 to 12 percent. Each reward family has a distinct and predictable set of blind spots, and inexpensive database-level checks that need no language model calls detect 45 to 60 percent of semantic errors. Controlled training simulations confirm that executiononly reward leaves output-preserving errors untouched, whereas a signal-grounded reward removes them even when the detectors are noisy.

articles.title: From Patterns to Threats: A Deep Learning Model for Anomaly Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems
articles.summary: Cyber-physical systems increasingly rely on interconnected sensing, communication, and control components, creating a need for reliable detection of abnormal behavior. This study proposes a Deep…
articles.abstract: Cyber-physical systems increasingly rely on interconnected sensing, communication, and control components, creating a need for reliable detection of abnormal behavior. This study proposes a Deep Autoencoder for anomaly detection using the Edge-IIoTset dataset. After preprocessing the full dataset, 2,219,201 observations and 38 numerical features were retained. The proposed model employed a 38-24-12-6-12-24-38 encoder-decoder architecture and was trained exclusively on normal observations to learn representative patterns of expected system behavior. Anomaly decisions were based on reconstruction error, with the classification threshold selected independently from validation data by maximizing the F1-score. To assess model stability, five independent runs were conducted using different random seeds, and results were reported as mean plus or minus standard deviation. The proposed Deep Autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 0.9195 plus or minus 0.0061, precision of 0.9602 plus or minus 0.0204, recall of 0.7348 plus or minus 0.0095, F1-score of 0.8325 plus or minus 0.0121, ROC-AUC of 0.8825 plus or minus 0.0339, and PR-AUC of 0.8640 plus or minus 0.0286. Compared with a Simple Autoencoder baseline, the proposed model improved recall and F1-score while reducing the false positive rate. The results demonstrate that the proposed reconstruction-based representation learning approach can provide an effective and reproducible method for detecting anomalous behavior in cyber-physical environments.

articles.title: Autonomous Multireference Quantum Chemistry with Artificial Intelligence Agents
articles.summary: Accurately describing chemical reactions that involve strongly correlated electrons remains a major challenge in computational chemistry. Multireference electronic structure methods can address this…
articles.abstract: Accurately describing chemical reactions that involve strongly correlated electrons remains a major challenge in computational chemistry. Multireference electronic structure methods can address this challenge, but their application requires expert decisions that are di!cult to automate, particularly when the electronic structure changes as chemical bonds form and break. Here we introduce CASPER, an autonomously agentic workflow that performs multireference calculations along chemical reaction pathways. CASPER combines chemical knowledge, electronic structure calculations, and iterative assessment to identify chemically meaningful active spaces and maintain their consistency as bonds form and break. We demonstrate its capabilities on five transition-metal reactions, for which CASPER generates consistent multireference potential energy profiles with minimal human intervention. Importantly, in two reactions, CASPER identifies critical electronic-structure problems that an independent Claude session fails to recognize without the structured workflow. These include an electronic-state crossing and the exclusion of an orbital involved in bond breaking. Our results show the importance of combining language models with chemical knowledge and independent assessment of computational results. Beyond automating calculations, such agents have the potential to help researchers better understand the underlying physics and chemistry and open new opportunities for investigating complex chemical reactivity and generating high-quality quantum chemical data at scale.

articles.title: World Models and the Law
articles.summary: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an…
articles.abstract: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an environment changes over time and predicting the consequences of an action, and they are already used to steer robots and generate explorable worlds. This article asks how AI regulation in three major legal contexts, the European Union, California, and China, copes with the distinctive challenges they raise. I propose a definition and a taxonomy of world models based on who or what acts on their predictions, and identify the risks of misplaced reliance on them. I argue that existing rules tend to cover world models but leave three questions open, i.e., action provenance, trajectory validity, and the weight of simulated evidence, and recommend ways to fill these gaps.

articles.title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
articles.summary: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks…
articles.abstract: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.

articles.title: Particle Belief Representations for Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
articles.summary: Particle filters flexibly represent complex, multimodal beliefs but expose them as weighted, unordered sets incompatible with conventional fixed-dimensional policies. We study particle-belief…
articles.abstract: Particle filters flexibly represent complex, multimodal beliefs but expose them as weighted, unordered sets incompatible with conventional fixed-dimensional policies. We study particle-belief encodings as inputs to reinforcement-learning policies while holding belief estimation and policy optimization fixed. We compare statistical summaries, cumulant-generating-function (CGF) features, and permutation-invariant set encoders. Trainable encoders are learned end-to-end or pretrained through belief reconstruction or task-specific prediction. Across eight tasks, pooling-based set encoders and gradient CGF features are reliable end-to-end, while the Set Transformer achieves the highest performance with appropriate pretraining. Task-specific pretraining helps when its target captures decision-relevant belief structure, whereas reconstruction pretraining and latent alignment provide more selective benefits. For selecting and training particle-belief encoders in partially observable Markov decision processes, our results show that an encoding that reconstructs the belief well is not necessarily a good input for control.

articles.title: Weight Averaging at Small Budgets Confounds Formula-Labeled Pretraining in Microstructure-Property Regression: A Pre-Specified Study with Post Hoc Rechecks
articles.summary: Closed-form physics formulas can label synthetic microstructures at no cost, so supervised pretraining on those labels is an alternative to self-supervised pretraining when labels are scarce. One…
articles.abstract: Closed-form physics formulas can label synthetic microstructures at no cost, so supervised pretraining on those labels is an alternative to self-supervised pretraining when labels are scarce. One pre-specified protocol tests this on two public simulated benchmarks, two-phase conductivity and short-fiber stiffness: a ConvNeXt-Small is pretrained on 150,000 synthetic images by formula regression or masked reconstruction and fine-tuned on 100, 400, or 1,600 labels. Five fine-tuning seeds from one formula checkpoint have mean residual correlations of 0.994 (conductivity) and 0.999 (stiffness). On conductivity the formula network compresses its predictions (slope 0.64) and has four times the 400-label error of ImageNet initialization. Two confounds interact: the generator renders the low-conductivity phase with the opposite contrast polarity, and the exponential moving average (EMA; decay 0.995, no bias correction) still holds 16% of the initial weights after the 400-label schedule. Without the EMA the slope is 0.97, and over three subsets and five seeds the mismatched checkpoint has 1.4 times the ImageNet error (0.0119 versus 0.0084). Three pretraining runs per polarity leave the comparison inconclusive: matched means (0.0086, 0.0111, 0.0118) fall below mismatched means (0.0119, 0.0120, 0.0123) in aggregate (0.0105 versus 0.0121) but overlap on two of three subsets, and the matched spread (0.0032) exceeds the mismatched spread (0.0004). On stiffness without the EMA, formula pretraining lowers the 100-label error by 18% versus ImageNet over five seeds, including a re-initialized head, while ImageNet seeds also correlate at 0.992. Weight averages that start at the pretrained weights can dominate small-budget comparisons and should be rechecked at the last weights.

articles.title: Deep Discriminative Feature Fusion of Convolutional and Attention-Based Recurrent Representations for Subject-Independent ECG Stress Recognition
articles.summary: Stress has become a significant concern because of its negative impact on both physical and mental health and therefore drives the need for reliable automated systems to assess stress levels.…
articles.abstract: Stress has become a significant concern because of its negative impact on both physical and mental health and therefore drives the need for reliable automated systems to assess stress levels. Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals provide a non-invasive and objective measure of physiological stress responses and have emerged as a promising modality for continuous stress monitoring. While deep learning techniques have achieved encouraging results in ECG-based stress detection, many studies focus only on one type of feature representation, and therefore limit their ability to capture both the morphological patterns and temporal dynamics embedded in ECG signals. To address this limitation, in this paper, we propose three deep learning-based feature fusion frameworks for ECG-based stress classification. These are Residual Feature Fusion (RFF), Bidirectional Feature-Wise Cross-Attention Fusion (BFCAF), and a novel Cross-Attention Residual Fusion (CARF) framework that combines the strengths of residual learning and bidirectional cross-attention within a unified architecture. A 1D Convolutional Neural Network (1D-CNN) and a BiLSTM-Attention network are used to extract complementary morphological and temporal representations from ECG signals, respectively. The proposed fusion frameworks leverage these heterogeneous representations to improve feature interaction, information preservation, and stress discrimination. The proposed frameworks are evaluated using subject-independent Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSOCV) on the RML and WESAD datasets for three-class stress classification. Experimental results show that the proposed feature fusion methods consistently improve performance over individual CNN and BiLSTM models, with CARF achieving the highest accuracies of 83.1% and 77.91% on the RML and WESAD datasets, respectively.

articles.title: Semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash on H5N1 One Health questions
articles.summary: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information…
articles.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information during outbreaks. Before a chatbot's accuracy can be meaningfully assessed, its consistency must first be understood, so that any single response can be trusted as a fair representative of the model's behavior. We characterized the semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 (OpenAI) and Gemini 3 Flash (Google) on 15 H5N1 One Health questions sourced from social media discourse by adopting and extending a centroid-based evaluation framework. Each question was submitted 30 times and reformulated using five Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variants with 30 runs each, yielding 5,400 responses. Pairwise cosine similarity was computed on MPNet embeddings, with sensitivity analyses across three additional transformers. Statistical inference combined standard nonparametric tests (paired Wilcoxon and Friedman with Holm--Bonferroni correction) with inter-embedding agreement statistics (ICC(2,k) and Cronbach's $α$) introduced here as a methodological addition. Both models produced high mean consistency (0.93--0.97, rescaled to {[}0, 1{]}). GPT-5 showed reproducibility significantly higher than repeatability (W = 3.0, p = 0.0003), whereas for Gemini 3 Flash the two metrics were statistically indistinguishable (W = 42.0, p = 0.33). Differential Diagnosis ranked among the top two CoT framings for consistency in both models. The tested chatbots behave as semantically stable sources on H5N1 One Health questions, and the developed consistency evaluation framework is portable to other domains.

articles.title: Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering
articles.summary: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension.
articles.abstract: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance the usability and reliability of LLMs, emphasizing the ongoing importance of well-designed prompts in optimizing task performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of prompt patterns in maximizing LLM's potential, even as their capabilities continue to evolve.

articles.title: The Stigmergic Index: A Biomimetic Edge Centrality for Spatial Network Analysis
articles.summary: Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is a family of metaheuristics inspired by the pheromone-based navigation of real ants, a decentralized mechanism often associated with shortest-path discovery. Over the…
articles.abstract: Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is a family of metaheuristics inspired by the pheromone-based navigation of real ants, a decentralized mechanism often associated with shortest-path discovery. Over the past two decades, research has primarily focused on optimization tasks such as vehicle routing within a network. In this paper, we shift this perspective by using swarm intelligence to gather diagnostic information about the underlying network structure itself. Through decentralized exploration, we harness stigmergic dynamics to introduce a novel topological and behavioural metric: the Stigmergic Index. While sharing baseline structural properties with traditional betweenness centrality on simple grids, our index accounts for path polarization effects that can diverge from shortest-path-based assumptions.

articles.title: Designing Incoherent Multispectral Diffractive Optical Networks for Satellite Image Classification
articles.summary: Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These…
articles.abstract: Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These advantages are especially attractive for multispectral satellite imaging, where conventional workflows rely on transmitting high-dimensional image cubes to the ground for downstream electronic analysis. Here, we introduce a computationally efficient surrogate model-guided framework for designing incoherent multispectral diffractive optical networks that directly output class probabilities onboard, eliminating the need to capture and transfer the full multispectral data cube for ground-side inference. We first train a physically compatible surrogate model, represented by a non-negative fully connected model that accommodates a generalized detector readout, yielding a task-specific non-negative multispectral intensity transformation that can be transferred to an optical processor. We then synthesize its diffractive counterpart through data-free point-spread-function-based optimization under spatially incoherent illumination. Using this approach, we numerically demonstrate a six-spectral-channel diffractive classifier for tri-class satellite-scene recognition, achieving a blind-testing accuracy of 79.8% for artificial surface, water body, and vegetated land images, closely approaching the 81.8% accuracy of its surrogate. We further demonstrate a more compact three-spectral-channel design that numerically achieves 72.7% blind-testing accuracy, compared with 75.1% for its corresponding surrogate model. This surrogate model-guided strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compact, task-specific incoherent multispectral optical processors for resource-constrained remote-sensing inference.

articles.title: SARA: An Auditor-in-the-Loop LLM Recommender for Sustainability Reports
articles.summary: Auditing corporate sustainability reports requires assurance professionals to map a company-specific checklist drawn from roughly 1,700 regulatory requirements onto the relevant passages of lengthy,…
articles.abstract: Auditing corporate sustainability reports requires assurance professionals to map a company-specific checklist drawn from roughly 1,700 regulatory requirements onto the relevant passages of lengthy, repeatedly revised draft reports and to judge compliance. We present SARA (Sustainability Reporting Assistant), a human-in-the-loop recommender system delivered as a Microsoft Word add-in that recommends, for each requirement, the passages addressing it and predicts a compliance verdict while keeping the auditor in full control. SARA casts auditing as content-based recommendation over a fixed regulatory taxonomy and makes per-requirement large language model (LLM) matching cheaper, faster, and more accurate through topic-prediction filtering: on expert-annotated reports, it reduces matching cost about sixfold and runtime by 42% versus feeding the full report to the LLM. It is in production use across PwC Germany's sustainability-assurance practice.

articles.title: Task-Dependent Linguistic Measures in Aphasia Discourse: A Comparative Analysis of Narrative, Descriptive, and Procedural Speech
articles.summary: Background: Transcript-based measures such as word counts, lexical diversity and disfluency rates are widely used to describe language ability in aphasia. Each measure comes from a specific…
articles.abstract: Background: Transcript-based measures such as word counts, lexical diversity and disfluency rates are widely used to describe language ability in aphasia. Each measure comes from a specific elicitation task, and studies use different tasks, so values from different tasks may not be comparable. Aims: To test whether discourse tasks change these measures within the same speakers, and whether the measures follow a gradient from Procedural to Descriptive to Narrative discourse. Methods & Procedures: Baseline transcripts from 61 adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia were taken from the Fridriksson-2 corpus in AphasiaBank (POLAR trial, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03416738). Each speaker produced a Procedural (Sandwich), a Descriptive (Broken Window) and a Narrative (Cinderella) sample in one session. A rule-based pipeline extracted 13 measures, 10 of which were common enough to test. Friedman, Page and Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction were used, with a speaker-grouped Random Forest classifier as a supporting check. Outcomes & Results: Total words and number of different words followed the full gradient, but the step from Procedural to Descriptive was small. For most other measures, Narrative stood apart, while Descriptive and Procedural did not differ. Among the 31 speakers with at least 25 words in every task, filler rate, repetition rate and total disfluency density were higher in Narrative than in both other tasks. The classifier reached an accuracy of 0.61 (always guessing the most common task would give 0.41), mainly by recognizing Narrative samples. Conclusions: Discourse tasks are not interchangeable, and expressing disfluencies per word does not remove the task effect. The task should be reported with every measure, and values should be compared only within the same task.

articles.title: Ask Again: Answer-List Instability in Generative Engines
articles.summary: Visibility in generative search engines is measured by which entities appear in responses, and in what order. Ask an engine the same question twice and the answer list can change: a different…
articles.abstract: Visibility in generative search engines is measured by which entities appear in responses, and in what order. Ask an engine the same question twice and the answer list can change: a different ordering, or different items altogether. Across 60,000 responses, we find that answers to the same prompt name a different first item 32% of the time, and even two answers with the same items disagree on which comes first. The first position is a measurement target of its own. A "clear leader" emerges after seven or eight runs, which are the budgets recommended for brand and source monitoring, but a "close leader" only about half the time. After 25 runs, a close leader is identified only 60% of the time. Variability between engines is larger than within the same engine. For open-ended prompts, the gap is more than double that for determinate ones. Search queries and cited sites observed leave most of the disagreement unexplained. Visibility measurement should report, for each engine, which items appear and how often each comes first, each with its own quantification of uncertainty.

articles.title: What Quality Engineers Need to Know About Generative AI: Structured Data Extraction
articles.summary: In this expository paper, we explain how quality engineers can use large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for structured data extraction. We introduce the relevant concepts,…
articles.abstract: In this expository paper, we explain how quality engineers can use large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for structured data extraction. We introduce the relevant concepts, discuss structured extraction from a measurement-system perspective, and demonstrate its implementation in R and Python. We then present two freely available web-based applications (apps): (a) extracting information from automotive recall notices and (b) monitoring quality engineering research on arXiv. To ensure the accuracy of our AI-driven structured extraction, human evaluators validated the results. In the first app, four reviewers assessed information extracted from 30 recall notices using two models, with 98.6% of the 720 field-level ratings judged fully correct. In the second app, 21 authors evaluated information extracted from 45 of their arXiv papers. All paper summaries were rated mostly correct or correct, although the evaluations identified problems with some classification fields and mathematical expressions. These results demonstrate the practical potential of structured data extraction while emphasizing the need to validate the extracted information. We make both apps and their source code publicly available so that readers can adapt the approach to their own applications.

articles.title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
articles.summary: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional…
articles.abstract: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. The framework is designed with three key objectives: (i) reducing manual annotation by harnessing prompt-based zero-shot and few-shot capabilities of modern LLMs, (ii) flexibly parsing diverse document formats (i.e., HTML, PDF, TXT, and JSON), and (iii) improving accessibility for non-expert users by automatically inducing schemas from document collections, which can then be refined for extraction. We evaluate Trallie with open-weight LLMs on FDA 510(k) documents and on movie and university websites from SWDE. It outperforms previously reported systems when the target attributes are provided for text extraction and is competitive when it must discover attributes for the schema automatically. The project is available at https://github.com/PiSchool/trallie

articles.title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation
articles.summary: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle…
articles.abstract: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films' Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.

articles.title: Synthetic Twins: Closing the Gap Between TTS Test Sets and Real Recordings in Turkish ASR Evaluation
articles.summary: Speech synthesized by text-to-speech engines is a low-cost substitute for recorded test sets in automatic speech recognition, yet an off-the-shelf synthetic test set is worth only a few dozen real…
articles.abstract: Speech synthesized by text-to-speech engines is a low-cost substitute for recorded test sets in automatic speech recognition, yet an off-the-shelf synthetic test set is worth only a few dozen real recordings for estimating the real error rate of a recognizer. This paper examines which properties of real recordings are missing from synthetic speech and how much of the gap can be closed. For 507 Turkish Common Voice recordings, synthetic twins are built: a ladder of synthetic copies that adds, one factor at a time, the pitch of the speaker, a clone of the same speaker, the real recording channel and the speaking rate. At each step, the agreement between ASR behaviour on the copy and on the real recording is measured. Across three zero-shot cloning engines and panels of six and 19 recognizers, the speaker clone is the step that improves agreement on which sentences are hard, raising the Spearman correlation from .41 to .55 for Chatterbox. Matching the channel or adding generic noise corrects the error level when the synthetic speech is easier than real speech. The twin with the highest worth is equivalent to 70 to 122 real recordings, depending on the recognizer panel, compared with about 9 for a stock voice. The findings replicate on VoxForge, a second corpus in which speaker identity is known rather than inferred: the clone raises sentence agreement from .31 to .50 and the worth from 8 to about 50 recordings. Agreement on which sentences are hard is distinct from agreement on how hard they are. The paper concludes with a practical recipe and a reporting checklist for synthetic ASR test sets.

articles.title: Empirical Margin Sensitivity: An Interventional Neuron-Level Probe of Post-Trained Medical LLMs
articles.summary: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support…
articles.abstract: Medical post-training raises benchmark accuracy, but accuracy does not show which internal components a model's decisions depend on, or whether components that support one benchmark also support another. We apply the weight-space intervention paradigm of ROME and MEMIT at the granularity of one MLP down-projection column. Our measurement, Empirical Margin Sensitivity (EMS), replaces each coordinate magnitude of a column by its mean while preserving the column's sign pattern and L1 scale, and records the resulting change in the logit margin between the correct option and its hardest-wrong competitor. This isolates the margin's dependence on a column's fine-grained coordinate structure while the column stays in place. We discover high-EMS columns (anchors) on MedQA in ten public checkpoints (four general-purpose bases and six medical post-trained variants) across the Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and AFM families, and measure the same columns on MedMCQA and PubMedQA. Mean-ablating each discovered anchor set lowers MedQA accuracy in all six post-trained models, by 6 to 28 points. In the two pure-SFT checkpoints, crushing anchors raises the PubMedQA margin on correctly answered items (negative EMS), and anchors with this property sit significantly deeper than the same model's other anchors; the four checkpoints trained with RL or mixed recipes show positive PubMedQA EMS and no significant depth shift. The depth association recurs in each of three held-out checkpoints. Because the checkpoints differ in data and pipeline as well as objective, we report these as per-checkpoint observations.

articles.title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to…
articles.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

articles.title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
articles.summary: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and…
articles.abstract: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

articles.title: Auxiliary Clues Aware's Geometry Problem Solving
articles.summary: Geometry Problem Solving (GPS) serves as a rigorous test of the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly when solutions require auxiliary constructions…
articles.abstract: Geometry Problem Solving (GPS) serves as a rigorous test of the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly when solutions require auxiliary constructions absent from the input diagram. However, explicit diagramming methods suffer from unstable image generation quality and cascading errors, while existing implicit attention mechanisms primarily focus on visible elements, limiting their ability to support reasoning that requires additional geometric constructions. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{AuxCA} (Auxiliary-Clues-Aware GRPO), a reinforcement learning framework that helps models learn transferable auxiliary-construction strategies that can be applied beyond the training domain without explicit diagram generation at inference time. Specifically, we introduce Auxiliary Clues Dependency (\textbf{ACD}) to quantify the influence of auxiliary visual clues on token generation and integrate it into GRPO through fine-grained advantage weighting. Furthermore, we incorporate an auxiliary incentive reward to encourage the effective use of auxiliary geometric clues in correct solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AuxCA-8B outperforms the explicit-plotting baseline Bagel-Canvas and achieves competitive performance with leading proprietary models on auxiliary-dependent plane geometry problems. Improvements on analytic geometry, solid geometry, and external benchmarks further suggest that the learned strategies can transfer beyond the training domain. Code is available at https://github.com/fukua23/AuxCA

articles.title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax
articles.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training…
articles.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. We study W4A4 quantization under the deployed decoder and find that the decoder determines both where quantization harms accuracy and what it costs. Irreversible errors enter chiefly through forced commitments, made when no position clears the threshold: they are a minority of commitments but carry most quantization-induced flips. Quantization also levies a parallelism tax, extra forward passes per response: by compressing top logit gaps, it pushes positions below the threshold while leaving predictions largely intact. We propose DECAL, which reweights layer-wise calibration by a commitment-risk prior measured on the deployed decoder, and an argmax-preserving commit temperature that recovers the tax. On LLaDA and Dream, DECAL attains the best average accuracy among W4A4 methods, with lower run-to-run variance than the closest existing calibration method.

articles.title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models
articles.summary: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world…
articles.abstract: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

articles.title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero
articles.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures…
articles.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.

articles.title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? An Empirical Study of Decoupled Knowledge and Generation Trajectories in Clinical LLMs
articles.summary: Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy…
articles.abstract: Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via \textit{MCQA} and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across $18$ checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned \textit{Qwen} models ($0.5B$ to $8B$), adapted to German medicine with \textit{CPT} and \textit{SLERP} merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching $90\%$ of their total gain after a median of $1.7B$ tokens versus $3.5B$ for \textit{MCQA}. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at $1.9B$ tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while \textit{MCQA} knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.

articles.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
articles.summary: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However,…
articles.abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

articles.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
articles.summary: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale…
articles.abstract: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans diverse mathematical domains and includes 69 historical pairs. We evaluate six language models with Direct and ReForm prompts on all 197 inputs against final human-reviewed reference labels. GPT-6.1 Sol with Direct prompting achieves the highest reported accuracy of 0.827 and misalignment-detection F1 of 0.844; the effects of prompting vary across models. LeanReviewBench provides a testbed for reviewing semantic correspondence in existing mathematical formalization projects. LeanReviewBench is available at https://github.com/MechMath/LeanReviewBench.

articles.title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift
articles.summary: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information…
articles.abstract: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.

articles.title: DUET: Dual-MDL Unsupervised Entropy-Trie Segmentation for Low-Resource Languages
articles.summary: Morphological segmentation, the task of decomposing words into constituent morphemes, becomes particularly challenging under extreme data scarcity, a regime that can arise in language documentation…
articles.abstract: Morphological segmentation, the task of decomposing words into constituent morphemes, becomes particularly challenging under extreme data scarcity, a regime that can arise in language documentation and linguistic reasoning. This difficulty stems from existing approaches' reliance on annotated data, external resources, or recurring patterns that emerge only in larger corpora. To address this limitation, we propose Dual-MDL Unsupervised Entropy-Trie Segmentation (DUET), a deterministic unsupervised algorithm that decouples structural candidate generation from statistical candidate ranking. DUET combines branching entropy with recursive paradigm discovery to generate linguistically plausible candidate segmentations, then ranks them using a dual minimum description length (MDL) criterion: a corpus-level objective rewards morpheme reuse, while a construction-tree objective guards against over-segmentation. On the SIGMORPHON 2023 interlinear glossing shared task, DUET outperforms unsupervised baselines in Morpheme F1 under both the standard and simulated extremely low-resource settings, while providing broader candidate coverage. Augmenting prompts with DUET segmentations improves performance on a linguistic reasoning benchmark, yielding the best overall results among the evaluated segmentation methods.

articles.title: VADE: A Verifiable Agent Data Engine from Professional Sources
articles.summary: Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this…
articles.abstract: Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this success to other professional domains, such as law and finance, is not straightforward: many agent tasks involve open-ended analysis, making outcomes hard to verify and, in turn, hard to use as scalable supervision.
