Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.

articles.title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
articles.summary: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR)…
articles.abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.

articles.title: SparQ4D: Learning to Act through Sparse 4D Queries
articles.summary: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision…
articles.abstract: Successful manipulation requires a policy to understand where things are and how they will move, yet action demonstrations leave this spatiotemporal structure implicit. While explicit 4D supervision has proven effective, reducing the cost of dense 4D prediction remains challenging. This paper introduces \method, a lightweight yet expressive decoder that efficiently injects holistic 4D scene understanding into policies and improves success rates. At its core is a query-based decoder attached to a pretrained policy, which casts many spatialtemporal tasks into one unified interface (e.g. depth, 2D/3D point motion, multi-view correspondence, and hand-eye relations). This design enables efficient training and inference without sacrificing expressivity: the policy learns rich 4D structure from a small number of sampled queries during training, while the decoder can be removed at inference with zero additional overhead. Across multiple backbones, simulated environments, and real-world settings, \method achieves state-of-the-art manipulation performance, outperforming competing methods while training up to $5\times$ faster. Probing analyses further reveal that this 4D structure is recoverable from the policy.

articles.title: Grounded in Contact: Reducing Floating and Interpenetration Artifacts with Multimodal Skill-Effect Models
articles.summary: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing,…
articles.abstract: Learning to predict the effects of contact-rich manipulation skills requires models that represent distinct outcome modes rather than a single expected result. Even for basic skills such as pushing, picking, and placing, small variations in contact conditions or object geometry can produce qualitatively different object motions under nearly identical states and actions. Deterministic and Gaussian models tend to average over these alternatives or represent them as a single broad distribution, obscuring distinct modes such as sliding, toppling, and rotating. We study probabilistic skill-effect models that learn multimodal distributions over object pose changes given partial point clouds and actions. We instantiate this abstraction with three representative model classes: mixture density networks, state tokenization, and flow matching, each paired with latent dynamics for next-step prediction. Across diverse objects and skills, explicitly multimodal models predict which outcome occurs more accurately than deterministic and Gaussian baselines. In planning, flow matching significantly improves task success over the deterministic baseline on every skill and achieves the highest success on every multi-step sequence. On a real robot, probabilistic models succeed at pick about twice as often as the deterministic baseline, providing evidence that probabilistic skill effects offer a practical abstraction for reasoning and planning under uncertainty.

articles.title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire…
articles.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.

articles.title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning
articles.summary: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing…
articles.abstract: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.

articles.title: Feedback Completion Certificates for Repeated Dwell Tasks with Time Windows
articles.summary: An inspection robot may owe several measurements at the same station, each with a different window in which a dwell can begin. We ask what a feedback controller must retain about earlier visits to…
articles.abstract: An inspection robot may owe several measurements at the same station, each with a different window in which a dwell can begin. We ask what a feedback controller must retain about earlier visits to guarantee all remaining deadlines under bounded disturbances. For a common spatial predicate and dwell length, removing redundant windows orders the remaining obligations by both endpoints. On every history without an expired obligation, the served windows form a suffix. One boundary and one capped run length therefore preserve the future satisfaction of the original task. On a verified library of branching motion primitives we use this state to recover a feedback policy. For one task type a scalar threshold per run length suffices, with work linear in the number of listed branches per time layer for fixed dwell. Multiple types require a joint recursion. On a quadrotor inspection library the threshold sweep reduced the cost of constructing a reusable full-domain policy, while a sparse Boolean baseline answered a single initial query faster. In a two-station MuJoCo patrol, three task-aware filters all met every window in twelve paired runs each. Of eight initially certified runs, the completion filter retained the certificate in all eight, compared with three for safety-only filtering.

articles.title: Representation Alignment Is Only as Good as the Teacher's Behavioral Structure
articles.summary: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or…
articles.abstract: Recent works align the intermediate features of vision-language-action (VLA) models with frozen vision encoders during fine-tuning, hoping to inject additional priors such as 3D awareness or affordances. Unlike in image generation, where teachers for representation alignment (REPA) are assessed with encoder-intrinsic metrics, teachers for VLAs are still chosen largely by heuristics. We show that this practice is unreliable: across 14 teachers and 16 manipulation tasks, under matched training budgets, no off-the-shelf vision encoder improves the clean success rate of $π_{0.5}$ by more than 1 point, and all of them reduce its success rate under perturbations by 10 to 39 points. Neither global semantics nor spatial structure, the criteria used in image generation, predicts which teachers help. We therefore propose the behavioral structure metric (BSM), which measures whether states that are close in a teacher's feature space are followed by similar expert actions within the same task. BSM correlates strongly with success rate under perturbations ($r=0.87$), and every off-the-shelf vision encoder scores below $π_{0.5}$ itself. Based on it, we introduce Behavior-Aware VLA Alignment (BAVA), a general VLA alignment protocol that favors vision encoders whose BSM exceeds the student's and stops alignment early according to the student's BSM during training. On SmolVLA, BAVA matches continuous alignment with one third of the alignment budget, and improves the average success rate by 4.6 points over unaligned fine-tuning. Our results suggest that representation alignment benefits VLAs only when the teacher encodes rich behaviorally relevant structure.

articles.title: A colour-marker tracker for pose estimation of slender surgical instruments: vision-language-model-guided adaptive colour calibration
articles.summary: Slender surgical instruments need small, narrow markers for camera-based pose estimation. A colour-stripe marker fits this requirement, but its colours in the image drift from the design values with…
articles.abstract: Slender surgical instruments need small, narrow markers for camera-based pose estimation. A colour-stripe marker fits this requirement, but its colours in the image drift from the design values with lighting, printing and camera settings. Because the colours can only be corrected after the marker has been found, methods that rely on the design colours face a circular problem. We propose vision-language-model (VLM)-based adaptive colour calibration and compare it with two rule-based methods, which re-measure the colours from detections made with the design colours: Initial colour update does so once after tracking starts, and Colour adaptation continuously during tracking. VLM guidance uses a fine-tuned VLM to find the markers without relying on the design colours and builds the colour profile from their pixels. Recall/F1 (%) for Initial colour update, Colour adaptation and VLM guidance were 92.0/95.7, 87.8/93.3 and 98.2/99.1 on 672 synthetic image pairs; 51.3/67.2, 48.8/65.0 and 83.8/87.0 on eight degraded laboratory videos; and 38.9/55.2, 19.7/29.7 and 100/100 on a surgical-robot (da Vinci) video with strongly shifted colours. In that video the rule-based methods never found the purple/cyan marker, whereas VLM guidance found all 234 markers with no false positives. In a simulation, the hue boundary between the two stripes moved by less than 0.1 pixel for exposure gains of 0.5-2.0, compared with 2.9-4.0 pixels for a boundary found with a fixed brightness threshold. When the degradation is mild, the rule-based methods, which need no training and no GPU, are sufficient. When the colours change greatly, the gain comes from a VLM-guided candidate search that does not rely on the design colours. Combining colour-stripe markers with adaptive colour calibration enables tracking of slender surgical instruments with small markers.

articles.title: Self-Refining VLA Sampling
articles.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves…
articles.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically use flow-based generative modeling to learn a rich, often multimodal, distribution of robot actions. Generating samples from flow-based methods involves iteratively updating random noise, and distinct noise samples from the same state can result in distinct trajectories and task outcomes. Existing test-time scaling methods improve action chunk generation via selection, aggregation, or correction, but commonly require the generation of large ensembles of candidates or the training of an external corrector. We adapt Predict-and-Perturb (P&P), a self-refinement procedure for flow-based models originally used for mode-seeking in video generation, to the robotics domain. We find that applying P&P to VLA models requires modifications to the refinement process used in video generation due to differences in the underlying structure of the data. Across 400 episodes of LIBERO evaluated using SmolVLA, P&P improves upon the stock baseline by 5.3 percentage points. Further, episode-level P\&P uncertainty correlates strongly with task failure (AUC 0.851).

articles.title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
articles.summary: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force…
articles.abstract: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.

articles.title: Scenario Compliant Indoor Pedestrian Trajectory Reconstruction from Partial Observation
articles.summary: Pedestrian trajectory reconstruction is vital for applications ranging from security surveillance to indoor navigation. While existing probabilistic and generative frameworks have shown success in…
articles.abstract: Pedestrian trajectory reconstruction is vital for applications ranging from security surveillance to indoor navigation. While existing probabilistic and generative frameworks have shown success in outdoor GPS-based trajectory imputation, they often fail in indoor settings where movement is strictly governed by dense geometric constraints such as walls and corridors. Standard models typically treat trajectories as unconstrained coordinate sequences, leading to physically infeasible paths with high collision rates. To address this, we propose a map-conditioned generative framework based on conditional diffusion models. Our approach explicitly integrates dense scenario maps as structured spatial inputs via a CNN-based encoder, allowing environmental geometry to guide the iterative denoising process. Furthermore, we employ an endpoint-aware mechanism by embedding observations (start and end points) directly into the scenario map, providing critical spatial anchors through image-level features. Experiments on simulated indoor trajectories and the real-world Shopper trajectory dataset, with three training seeds, show that our method achieves the lowest errors among the compared generative methods. Scene conditioning reduces the collision and invalid rates by 19\% and 46\% on the simulated dataset, whereas on real shopper data the gains are consistent but small, mainly because the model rarely learns to route around obstacles between the endpoints. Compared with a shortest-path planner, which never collides, our method better captures the variability of real motion (31\% lower CRPS), but the timing of stops is reconstructed only partially. These results show that explicit environmental context improves physical consistency, while reconstructing realistic human motion in real indoor spaces remains challenging. Our code is available at https://github.com/dang-qi/trajectory_reconstruction

articles.title: Specification-Aware Sparse Differentiation: Planning under Signal Temporal Logic with Sparsemax Robustness
articles.summary: Gradient-based optimal control under a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification involves solving a nonlinear program whose constraints are smoothed robustness functions of the trajectory, and…
articles.abstract: Gradient-based optimal control under a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification involves solving a nonlinear program whose constraints are smoothed robustness functions of the trajectory, and automatic differentiation without knowledge of sparsity computes the Jacobian and the Hessian that its solver needs in full. This often renders the problem computationally intractable. The dynamics and the specification prescribe a sparsity pattern through the STL syntax, the windows of the temporal operators and the variables that the predicates read. Standard tools such as CasADi recover this pattern by structural detection. In this work, we propose a method to prescribe such a pattern directly from the task specification. We show that our method allows us to exploit SparseMax, a recently proposed smooth robustness operator that is certifiably sparse and sound. Its derivative is exactly zero at every operand at or below a data-dependent threshold, which structural detection cannot see. We derive the patterns that expose this trajectory-dependent sparsity to sparse automatic differentiation, with a margin test for their reuse and Hessians confined to the variables of each constraint's support. We demonstrate the method on a dual-arm coordination task in which two arms share a hand-off zone divided into cells and one until constraint per scheduled visit keeps the other arm out of a cell until the visitor has left it. The two scenes are a zone of five cells and a circle of 64 cells, with single solves and closed-loop re-planning on a rigid-body simulation. Our exact-Hessian interior-point solves are up to 27 times faster than those with the sound log-sum-exp robustness in CasADi and IPOPT.

articles.title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
articles.summary: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable…
articles.abstract: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.

articles.title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
articles.summary: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an…
articles.abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

articles.title: RSLaA: Self-Reconfiguring Roadside LiDARs as Agents for 3D Traffic Perception
articles.summary: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because…
articles.abstract: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.

articles.title: A2I-VLA: A Two-Stage Vision-Language-Action model with Semantic-Physical Alignment and Integration
articles.summary: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these…
articles.abstract: Force and tactile feedback provide essential information about physical interactions in contact-rich manipulation that visual observations alone cannot reliably capture.However, integrating these signals into vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging owing to the representational gap between visual-language semantics and physical measurements.To address this challenge, we propose A2I-VLA, a two-stage VLA framework that first learns semantically Aligned force-tactile representations and then Integrates them into a VLA model.In Stage I, a cross-modal alignment loss is introduced to promote correspondence between semantic and physical representations. The tactile and force feature streams are then integrated through a hierarchical multimodal fusion network, and the resulting representations are jointly supervised by future wrench and action prediction losses. The former encourages the model to anticipate physical responses, while the latter associates force-tactile observations with task-relevant manipulation behaviors.In Stage II, a gated cross-attention bridge module adaptively integrates the hierarchical physical features learned in Stage I into the VLA model to guide action generation.Real-world experiments demonstrate that the proposed A2I-VLA significantly outperforms the baseline PI05 across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, improving the success rate from 70% to 95%.

articles.title: $ζ_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
articles.summary: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while…
articles.abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $ζ_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $ζ_0$ built on $Ψ_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/

articles.title: DriveOddsBench: Are Driving Video World Models Aligned with Real-World Odds?
articles.summary: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are…
articles.abstract: Video world models predict how a scene will evolve, and their sampled futures are increasingly used in place of the real one, from planning to simulation. These uses assume that the samples are aligned with real-world odds, with each future appearing among them as often as it would follow the same history in reality, yet current evaluations only score how real each sample looks. Testing this assumption on real driving data is hard for three reasons. Each recorded history has only one real future, so the true probabilities are unknown. Physical quantities must be read from video, where reading errors can look like model errors. Finally, the many possible analyses invite selective reporting. We introduce DriveOddsBench, a pre-registered benchmark that addresses all three. First, if the samples follow the real distribution, the rank of the real outcome among them is uniform in every history, so pooled ranks test them without probability labels. Second, one validated instrument reads the same quantities, such as the lead-vehicle gap and the ego motion, from the generated futures and from the real future, which first passes through the world model's autoencoder so that both are read alike. Third, all confirmatory analyses were frozen before any test clip was measured. We test eleven general and driving world models on 200 held-out Argoverse 2 histories in five scenario families, with 35,200 generated futures. None is aligned, and every model underestimates its uncertainty. The real outcome falls outside the range of all 16 samples in 28-61% of cases instead of the 11.8% expected under the real distribution. Five models are significantly skewed, in opposite directions, and the largest errors are in the ego motion. Nine models beat climatology without being aligned, and among these models neither type nor scale predicts which comes closest.

articles.title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
articles.summary: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to…
articles.abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

articles.title: InfoField3D: Differentiable Information Field for Embodied Task-Oriented View Planning
articles.summary: Effective task execution requires embodied agents to select observation positions that provide sufficient task-relevant information. Existing approaches typically predict viewpoints with learned…
articles.abstract: Effective task execution requires embodied agents to select observation positions that provide sufficient task-relevant information. Existing approaches typically predict viewpoints with learned models or score discrete candidates, but they either struggle to incorporate new constraints such as reachability or require extensive candidate evaluation to search. We introduce InfoField3D, which lifts geometry-bound information into a differentiable analytic field, whose value at each 3D observation position represents the task-required information accessible there. It uses low-order spherical harmonics to encode directional information responses and analytic line integrals of Gaussian occupancy functions to model occlusion along lines of sight. This formulation casts task-driven camera placement as a well-studied constrained continuous optimization problem, enabling both flexible incorporation of constraints through the feasible domain and efficient viewpoint search even in the presence of occlusion. Experiments show that InfoField3D compactly preserves the pointwise information landscape with high fidelity and generally recommends higher-quality, more robust viewpoints at lower search cost than the evaluated baselines. Controlled evaluations with a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy further suggest that the recommended views can improve downstream task performance under information-limited initial viewpoints.

articles.title: Force2Act: A Force-Aware Visuomotor Policy for Generalizable Compliant Robot Manipulation
articles.summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to regulate the force it applies, not only where it moves. Existing force-aware policies learn this force from demonstrations and therefore reproduce the…
articles.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to regulate the force it applies, not only where it moves. Existing force-aware policies learn this force from demonstrations and therefore reproduce the force levels they were trained on, which fails once the interaction demands more force than any demonstration. We present Force2Act, a hybrid force-position policy built on two complementary mechanisms. A global force policy plans the motion and the interaction force once per action chunk, with force represented relative to the measured interaction, so that the planned force scales with the load. Between planning steps, a reactive compliance policy, termed Mixture of Force Experts, identifies at every control step the force expert that governs the interaction and regulates the force through it, so that the contact holds when it changes within a chunk. We further introduce Force2Act-Bench, a simulation benchmark of five contact-rich tasks that gives the community a common and repeatable way to test force-aware policies and measure how well they regulate the interaction force. Force2Act achieves an overall success rate of 93.8%, compared with 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and its reactive regulation reduces the failures on block pivoting from 30 to 10 of 150 trials. On a real robot, Force2Act reaches an average success rate of 94.2% over four tasks, against at most 27.5% for the baselines.

articles.title: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
articles.summary: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a…
articles.abstract: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.

articles.title: FunGrasp-Zero: Field-Conditioned Graph Attention Policy for Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Functional Grasping
articles.summary: Dexterous functional grasping is critical for robotic tool use, yet current dexterous hands exhibit substantial morphological diversity. This hardware heterogeneity makes cross-embodiment functional…
articles.abstract: Dexterous functional grasping is critical for robotic tool use, yet current dexterous hands exhibit substantial morphological diversity. This hardware heterogeneity makes cross-embodiment functional grasping a fundamental but largely unexplored problem. Existing functional grasping methods use retargeted hand poses as guidance, tying task representation to a specific embodiment and failing to explicitly capture object-centric functional contact intent, limiting generalization across hands. To address this, we propose FunGrasp-Zero, a reinforcement learning framework for zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping. Instead of relying on embodiment-specific joint configuration, FunGrasp-Zero captures functional intent via an object-centric, cross-embodiment-consistent contact map, adapted to heterogeneous hands through morphological mapping. We construct a hand-object potential field from mapped contact regions, yielding attractive and repulsive guidance vectors. A Field-Conditioned Graph Attention Network (FC-GAT) leverages these vectors to coordinate multi-finger motion across hands, while a potential field reward guides fingers toward target regions and penalizes non-target collisions to enforce functional alignment and stability. We further establish X-FunBench for cross-embodiment functional grasping, evaluating both physical grasp success and functional intent preservation across hands. Evaluated on X-FunBench, our unified policy, co-trained on four embodiments, achieves 86% average grasp success rate across five unseen hands on novel objects. Deployed on four unseen physical hands (Leap, Inspire, Sharpa, Wuji) for novel object grasping, the policy achieves 80% average success rate without fine-tuning. To our knowledge, FunGrasp-Zero is the first RL-based framework to achieve zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping across unseen hands in both simulation and the real world.

articles.title: SpatialDuet: Bayesian task routing between a metric expert and a geometry expert for spatial intelligence
articles.summary: Embodied assistants and wearable devices need 3D spatial reasoning, and their limited hardware restricts them to small vision-language models (VLMs). Small spatial VLMs acquire different abilities…
articles.abstract: Embodied assistants and wearable devices need 3D spatial reasoning, and their limited hardware restricts them to small vision-language models (VLMs). Small spatial VLMs acquire different abilities from their training: a model trained on large spatial question sets estimates object and room sizes well, whereas a model with a 3D geometry encoder is better at relative directions and absolute distances. Instead of training a single model for all spatial tasks, as published methods do, we build one system that uses each frozen model for the tasks it handles best. We propose SpatialDuet, which pairs a metric expert with a geometry expert under a Bayesian task router. The metric expert is a data-driven spatial VLM run with three training-free modules: training-aligned sampling, metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding and per-type metric calibration. The geometry expert is a VLM with a 3D geometry encoder. For each question type, the router estimates from labelled development questions how likely each expert is to be better, and pools their answers with that probability as weight, in log space for numeric answers and over the option distributions for multiple-choice answers. Extensive experiments on four spatial benchmarks covering video and single images validate SpatialDuet; it outperforms the best published small VLMs by 3.17% on VSI-Bench and, excluding a model trained on CV-Bench-style data, by 1.44% on CV-Bench, without training any model weight.

articles.title: Implementation and Software-in-the-Loop Evaluation of a Trans-Domain Digital Twin Architecture for Autonomous Guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV Without Online GNSS
articles.summary: Autonomous UAV guidance in emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, and cargo transportation requires reliable navigation. However, satellite-based positioning may become unavailable or…
articles.abstract: Autonomous UAV guidance in emergency response, infrastructure monitoring, and cargo transportation requires reliable navigation. However, satellite-based positioning may become unavailable or unreliable in enclosed spaces, blind spots caused by natural obstacles and structures, and environments affected by radio interference and signal spoofing during electronic warfare. This study designs, implements, and evaluates a system based on a Trans-Domain Digital Twin (TDDT) for autonomous guidance of the Phoenix VTOL UAV. Independent navigation, flight dynamics, and meteorological models are coordinated within a cycle of state estimation, prediction, decision-making, command execution, and feedback. Data from inertial, magnetic, pressure, and airspeed sensors, together with environmental information, form the basis for estimation and prediction. Furthermore, a shared state, temporal synchronization, preservation of information provenance, and command traceability establish continuity between models and decisions. The system was tested with a simulated physical twin in a software-in-the-loop environment. Vertical takeoff, movement toward the destination, landing, and autonomous stopping were recorded, and the dynamic model was adjusted to a limited extent based on sensor-derived feedback. Separating the evaluation reference from navigation inputs enabled independent assessment of positioning error and computational performance. The results confirm operational coordination, decision traceability, and closed-loop guidance under the tested conditions, providing a reproducible platform for the development and evaluation of navigation without satellite-based positioning.

articles.title: Your Diffusion-Based Driving Planner Only Needs a Nudge
articles.summary: Diffusion-based planners capture the multimodality of human driving behavior well, yet covariate shift in closed-loop driving can lead them to generate trajectories that result in collisions or road…
articles.abstract: Diffusion-based planners capture the multimodality of human driving behavior well, yet covariate shift in closed-loop driving can lead them to generate trajectories that result in collisions or road departures. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning offers a promising way to tackle this issue, but applying it to diffusion-based planners is complicated by their iterative denoising process and receding-horizon execution. We find that small adjustments to the planned trajectories can prevent many of these unsafe outcomes. Motivated by this observation, we propose PlanNudge, which preserves the learned planning capabilities of a pretrained diffusion-based planner by freezing it and trains a lightweight policy that we call the nudge policy. At each planning step, the nudge policy outputs a nudge, a two-dimensional adjustment of the speed and curvature of the plan from the frozen planner. The nudge policy is a multilayer perceptron that predicts the nudge in a single forward pass, and both dimensions directly change the motion of the vehicle, so standard off-policy RL can train it in closed-loop simulation. We evaluate PlanNudge on nuPlan, a large-scale autonomous driving benchmark based on real-world driving data. In all six settings, PlanNudge matches or exceeds the final scores of the previous state-of-the-art RL finetuning method while using about one sixth as many environment steps and less than one fifth as much model compute. We also provide guidelines for reward shaping, value learning, and exploration when using off-policy RL to post-train autonomous driving planners. Our results are reported with means and standard deviations over six training runs. Project page: https://zerlinwang.github.io/plannudge/

articles.title: Less Rational, More Transparent: Censorship as (Robustly) Optimal Disclosure
articles.summary: Online platforms often control the information behind user decisions they want to influence, such as whether a driver accepts a trip or a buyer completes a purchase. A classical result in information…
articles.abstract: Online platforms often control the information behind user decisions they want to influence, such as whether a driver accepts a trip or a buyer completes a purchase. A classical result in information disclosure shows that a {\em censorship} policy is optimal for the platform: the platform pools all sufficiently favorable options under a common message, such as a quality badge, and reveals the rest individually. This result, however, presumes fully rational users. We study disclosure to boundedly rational users who follow the logit quantal response model and whose rationality level the platform may not know. Our results deliver a unifying message: less rational, more transparent. Neither bounded rationality nor uncertainty about it calls for a more complex policy; each changes only how much the platform should pool, and only toward greater transparency. When the rationality level is known, censorship remains optimal, and less rational users optimally receive at least as much information as more rational ones. When the rationality level is unknown, censorship remains robustly optimal under each of three criteria: the maximin ratio, maximin payoff, and minimax regret, and the robust censorship can be chosen to be at least as transparent as the policy designed for fully rational users. This additional transparency weakly benefits both parties and acts as insurance against behavioral uncertainty: rationality-robust censorship secures at least 89.96\% of the payoff attainable with knowledge of the user's rationality level, whereas the policy designed for fully rational users can secure as little as 50\%. Taken together, these results suggest that platforms can keep their badge-based disclosure but should narrow its coverage when users may be boundedly rational.

articles.title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values
articles.summary: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this…
articles.abstract: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID.

articles.title: Sub-Gaussian HDLSS Principal Component Analysis: High-Probability Theory and Numerical Evidence for NRM, CDM, and Block Noise Reduction
articles.summary: We study principal component analysis when the dimension d is much larger than the sample size n under an independent-factor sub-Gaussian model. The dual sample covariance is decomposed into a…
articles.abstract: We study principal component analysis when the dimension d is much larger than the sample size n under an independent-factor sub-Gaussian model. The dual sample covariance is decomposed into a finite-rank score matrix, an isotropic bulk shift, and a high-probability remainder governed by the bulk trace τ_0, Frobenius scale q_0, and largest noise eigenvalue b_0 = ||Λ_0||_{op}. This decomposition separates fixed-score HDLSS limits from joint limits in which n also grows. It shows that sequential noise reduction generally targets a score oracle containing a later-spike subtraction, while an oracle block correction avoids that subtraction when the signal rank is known. A parallel cross-data-matrix bound explains the benefit and cost of sample splitting. Reproducible Gaussian-factor simulations with 1,000 replications per configuration confirm the score-oracle approximation, the multi-spike subtraction, the separation between eigenvalue and eigenvector scales, and the population transition when n grows.

articles.title: Mirror Descent at the Edge of Stability
articles.summary: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/η$. We study this…
articles.abstract: In many deep learning settings, gradient descent has been shown to operate at the edge of stability -- a regime where the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian hovers around $2/η$. We study this phenomenon in mirror descent, a generalization of gradient descent. As mirror descent is non-Euclidean, existing explanations of the edge of stability phase do not extend to this setting. We generalize the existing notion of sharpness to introduce mirror sharpness, which measures the curvature of the loss with respect to the mirror potential. Empirically, we observe that the mirror sharpness hovers slightly above the $2/η$ threshold. Furthermore, we derive a dual central flow ODE for mirror descent that models iterates in continuous time at the onset of edge of stability. Our ODE provides insights into the difficulties of extending existing arguments for why sharpness stabilizes at $2/η$ from gradient descent to mirror descent in full generality.

articles.title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means
articles.summary: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have…
articles.abstract: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have enabled the embedding of shape data into Euclidean spaces, facilitating comparisons and machine learning tasks. Vector summaries that effectively capture topological structures are particularly useful for shape classification and unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering. We investigate the use of vectorized topological data for clustering through k-means, which partitions observations into a fixed number of groups by minimizing a squared-error loss function. By incorporating an element-wise weight-update step into the iterative k-means algorithm, we improve clustering performance on both simulated and real-world shape datasets. We show that estimating these weights reduces to a least-squares problem, requiring minimal additional computation while allowing flexible coefficient constraints. Our approach also substantially strengthens the negative correlation between the loss and clustering accuracy, improving the effectiveness of selecting among multiple clustering solutions based on the lowest loss. These improvements remain robust to changes in vector length and the number of initializations. Furthermore, weighted topological vector summaries exhibit stability under small structural perturbations, particularly when weight constraints are imposed. The proposed method offers a flexible alternative for clustering topological data, accommodating different k-means variants, vectorization methods, and weight constraints.

articles.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
articles.summary: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$…
articles.abstract: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

articles.title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
articles.summary: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease…
articles.abstract: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

articles.title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
articles.summary: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every…
articles.abstract: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

articles.title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
articles.summary: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit.…
articles.abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

articles.title: Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
articles.summary: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action…
articles.abstract: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.

articles.title: The Curved Exponential Family of Cylindrical Distributions: m-Projection, Curvature and a Test of the von Mises-Fisher Component
articles.summary: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in…
articles.abstract: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in it; this generalizes the Mardia-Sutton model. The family is a curved exponential family inside a regular family with Fisher-Bingham directions. We state necessary and sufficient conditions for the maximum-likelihood estimator to exist and be unique. The estimator is explicit except for one scalar root and is the m-projection (Kullback-Leibler projection) of the moment-matching member. Every moment it does not match is a function of one residual, the gap between the sample and fitted second moments of the direction. The squared length of this gap in the Fisher metric is the classical score test of von Mises-Fisher against Fisher-Bingham directions, due to Cox on the circle and extended by Mardia, Holmes and Kent. Specific here are this reading and the exact invariance of its law to the regression part. The exponential curvature lies only in the directions of the regression matrix. In closed form, the information lost on this matrix against the expected information is m-1 observations for uniform directions and (m+1)^2/(m-1) in the limit of high concentration; conditioning on the directions recovers it. Finite mixtures are identifiable. On buoy records the test rejects von Mises-Fisher directions, and generalized von Mises directions raise the held-out log-density by 0.45 nats per observation with one component.

articles.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
articles.summary: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d.
articles.abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

articles.title: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
articles.summary: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in…
articles.abstract: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|ψ|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $ψ$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2ρV/(1+ρ^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/λ$, from the photons alone.

articles.title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
articles.summary: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to…
articles.abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.

articles.title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics
articles.summary: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies,…
articles.abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies, including supplier delays and bottlenecks in order shipping. This work, conducted within the Horizon Europe project M4ESTRO, introduces a hybrid modelling approach combining graph theory and machine learning to represent supply chain logistics operations, with a focus on predicting delays in inbound flows between industrial suppliers and manufacturing entities. The various stages of order fulfilment are modelled through a formal mathematical framework, by defining disruption indicators computed from both historical and real-time data drawn from heterogeneous sources, including traffic and weather conditions and supplier dispatch readiness. Building on a graph-based representation of the supply chain, stochastic methods based on Markov chains are applied to estimate delivery times, detect schedule deviations, quantify prediction uncertainty, and produce interpretable metrics to support operational decision-making. Within the M4ESTRO project, the proposed framework was applied to build a web application for real-time tracking of inbound logistics, and was validated in a use case with an industrial project partner. The web application successfully enabled early detection of logistics disruptions along the supply chain and provided stakeholders with the visibility needed to act before delays propagated. The underlying model proved effective as the basis of a resilient, data-driven logistics tracking system, aligned with the digital transformation objectives of industry and with Manufacturing-as-a-Service paradigms.

articles.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
articles.summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on…
articles.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

articles.title: Do Larger Fully Connected Neural Networks Generalize Better?
articles.summary: Greater neural-network capacity does not necessarily yield better performance on unseen data. This study investigates whether a deeper, fully connected neural-network architecture generalizes better…
articles.abstract: Greater neural-network capacity does not necessarily yield better performance on unseen data. This study investigates whether a deeper, fully connected neural-network architecture generalizes better than a shallower architecture on the Fashion-MNIST dataset. We compare two architectures under two learning rates and two L2-regularization settings, producing eight configurations. The architectures contain 95,410 and 561,470 trainable parameters, respectively, an approximately 5.9-fold difference. Checkpoints and the final configuration are selected by validation loss, and all configurations are evaluated on a held-out test set. The selected larger configuration achieves 89.82% validation accuracy and 88.77% test accuracy. Selecting the lowest-validation-loss configuration within each architecture yields test accuracies of 88.77% and 88.52%, respectively, a difference of 0.25 percentage points. Across matched training settings, the larger architecture achieves higher test accuracy in only one of four comparisons. Class-level errors are concentrated among visually similar garment categories, and qualitative pixel-removal analyses suggest sensitivity to shape and boundaries. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing architectural capacity alone does not guarantee better generalization, highlighting the importance of considering optimization and regularization when selecting neural-network architectures.

articles.title: Which Model Belongs in the Loop? Evaluating Fitness Functions for Network Topology Optimization with a Quality-Diversity Algorithm
articles.summary: Network topology optimization (NTO) can reduce redispatch cost by rerouting power flows in transmission systems. To approach NTO, a complex combinatorial problem, gradient-free optimization…
articles.abstract: Network topology optimization (NTO) can reduce redispatch cost by rerouting power flows in transmission systems. To approach NTO, a complex combinatorial problem, gradient-free optimization algorithms that leverage diversity have shown promising results. These algorithms rely on frequent evaluations of candidate topologies by fitness functions. Recent work has shown that fast DC power flow-based fitness functions can serve this purpose. However, DC power flow fitness functions can misjudge the cost and feasibility of topologies, potentially leading to wrong operational decisions. Understanding the impact of fitness function accuracy on optimization performance is therefore crucial. This study compares the optimization performance of four fitness functions based on DC and AC power flow and on DC and AC optimal power flow. Furthermore, we propose a ranking-based metric to estimate the optimization performance of a fitness function on a curated dataset. Case studies cover the IEEE 118-bus case with 50 congested operating points and a 793-bus case for validation. Results show that optimal power flow-based fitness functions perform better in the optimization loop than power flow-based ones. Additionally, the results indicate that the metric can predict the optimization performance order of the fitness functions, but only if the distribution shift between the curated dataset and the search path of the optimization is small.

articles.title: Neural-Network Approximators for Low-Thrust Multi-Asteroid Rendezvous Optimization
articles.summary: Designing low-thrust multi-asteroid rendezvous missions requires the coupled selection of asteroid sequences, encounter epochs, and low-thrust trajectories. Lambert transfers support rapid beam…
