articles.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
articles.summary: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language…
articles.abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

articles.title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
articles.summary: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that…
articles.abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$) CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.

articles.title: Multiobjective household energy planning using evolutionary algorithms
articles.summary: This article presents the advances in the design and implementation of a recommendation system for planning the use of household appliances, focused on improving energy efficiency from the point of…
articles.abstract: This article presents the advances in the design and implementation of a recommendation system for planning the use of household appliances, focused on improving energy efficiency from the point of view of both energy companies and end-users. The system proposes using historical information and data from sensors to define instances of the planning problem considering user preferences, which in turn are proposed to be solved using a multiobjective evolutionary approach, in order to minimize energy consumption and maximize quality of service offered to users. Promising results are reported on realistic instances of the problem, compared with situations where no intelligent energy planning are used (i.e., Bussiness as Usual model) and also with a greedy algorithm developed in the framework of the reference project. The proposed evolutionary approach was able to improve up to 29.0% in energy utilization and up to 65.3% in user preferences over the reference methods.

articles.title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions
articles.summary: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and…
articles.abstract: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and draws the contour lines they imply. The contour map decomposes the evaluated region into peaks: in two dimensions a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, and in more dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates the peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. A memory of the explored peaks directs the search to new ones. The data-supported contours of each peak are extrapolated to zero size by an area law, exact for quadratic peaks and second-order accurate for smooth ones, that estimates a peak's location, height and shape before it is sampled. A contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) inserts contour steps with local search and peak memory into a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution or particle swarm optimization. A contour-assisted surrogate-assisted EA (CA-SAEA), for expensive problems, spends each evaluation on surrogate-screened offspring or on sampling around a peak, entered at the maximum of the interpolated surface. On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces the evaluations a plain GA needs by factors of 12 to 112; controls attribute its gain over classical memetic search to restarting local search on distinct peaks. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank, behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and the competition winner MVMO, although in 30 dimensions MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions and loses on 6; there the map beats sampling around the best point on 5 of 15 functions and loses on 3. Entering the peaks at their extrapolated locations brought no gain at these budgets, although, with enough samples, it improves the estimated heights on most two-dimensional functions.

articles.title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World
articles.summary: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the…
articles.abstract: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights. With a correct successor model, fixed exact role encoding and protected updates, the certified measure preserves the care boundary under arbitrary own reward. An explicit quotient condition transfers the finite certificate across the declared family, while two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identify when the role code ceases to suffice. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates. In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a world-model check at each action. A matched comparison reproduces a future-aware shield's decisions, whereas removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses. Reward and source-contamination thresholds, together with witness-falsification trials, identify the conditions on which the construction depends. The construction shows how learned care can survive further learning in a finite world under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution.

articles.title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
articles.summary: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers…
articles.abstract: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.

articles.title: A Multi-Parent Edge Assembly Crossover Driven Hybrid Genetic Algorithm for the Hamiltonian \textit{p}-Median Problem
articles.summary: The Hamiltonian \textit{p}-median problem seeks to partition the vertices of a graph into exactly $p$ disjoint cycles while minimizing their total cost. This paper presents a hybrid genetic algorithm…
articles.abstract: The Hamiltonian \textit{p}-median problem seeks to partition the vertices of a graph into exactly $p$ disjoint cycles while minimizing their total cost. This paper presents a hybrid genetic algorithm incorporating a multi-parent edge assembly crossover operator. The crossover combines a base solution with multiple donor solutions in a single recombination operation, thereby expanding the space of available edge exchanges. It uses virtual copies of the base solution to establish edge balance, together with an auxiliary directed graph and a budgeted search to construct valid AB-cycles. Extensive experiments on 215 benchmark instances across four sets show that the proposed algorithm improves the best-known solution values for 34 instances and matches those for another 168. Additional experiments indicate that a moderate number of parents provides beneficial diversity, whereas excessive parent counts, particularly when $p$ is large, lead to excessive population dispersion and hinder convergence.

articles.title: Before AI Agents Negotiate for Us: A Competitive Tournament of Rule-Based, Search, Optimization, Learned, and Language-Model Negotiators Under Scarcity
articles.summary: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with…
articles.abstract: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with whom. Prior strategy comparisons typically use isolated one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy behaves against several live rivals under a changing balance of supply and demand. We built nine negotiation architectures spanning rule-based, search-based, optimization-based, imitation-learning, and reinforcement-learning families, and ran all nine simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across all 36 exclusion pairs. In the balanced carrier market, an imitation-learned engine (ML2), a reinforcement-learning policy trained only on isolated negotiations (RL), and an expected-utility optimization engine (OPT) formed a statistically tied top group, and no architecture led in every condition and role. RL beat all eight carrier rivals when carriers were scarce, but its match rate collapsed from 62% to 16% when shippers were scarce and it had to compete with the other carrier agents for demand. A second reinforcement-learning policy trained against rival agents (RL2) kept its match rate above 91% in every condition, yet lost on realized payoff to all eight shipper-side rivals in two of the three conditions, traced to a confirmed train/deployment feature mismatch. We also tested nine large language models (LLMs), from 1 to 72 billion parameters, under the same protocol: they lost significantly to the two strongest engines (OPT2 and ML2) in 32 of 36 comparisons and won none. These results show that isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament exposes directly.

articles.title: Coverage-Aware Routing with Approximate Equilibrium Guarantees for Location-Diversity Vehicular Crowdsensing
articles.summary: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed. Location-diversity incentives pay vehicles…
articles.abstract: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed. Location-diversity incentives pay vehicles more to travel where few others go, but our earlier mechanism sets how far each vehicle deviates without optimizing collective coverage in route selection. We add this step in two stages. First, a non-cooperative game with diversity-weighted rewards yields each vehicle's equilibrium deviation. Second, the platform recommends to each vehicle a feasible route whose deviation is within a tolerance of this value, chosen to improve coverage. The coverage gain is monotone submodular, so a greedy router with local search attains at least half of the optimal gain over generated candidates. If every active vehicle has a candidate within a tolerance that is small relative to the aggregate deviation, the recommended routes form an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with $\varepsilon$ first order in the tolerance, or second order under a stronger condition. On London and Monaco road networks, the router achieves 99.4% and 98.9% of the optimal reduction in the coverage penalty on small instances and exceeds closest-length selection by up to 27.9 points. Under heterogeneous costs, uniform deviation needs compensation averaging 42% of the budget to give every vehicle nonnegative utility; the equilibrium targets need almost none. They also yield more coverage per unit of added travel in most settings and up to 22.6 more points at small budgets, an advantage that depends on placement and reverses at large budgets, where detour limits bind.

articles.title: Beyond Worst-Case Online Algorithms via Input Subsampling
articles.summary: We study whether classical competitive ratios survive input subsampling, when both the online algorithm and the offline optimum are evaluated on the same subsampled input. We consider the canonical…
articles.abstract: We study whether classical competitive ratios survive input subsampling, when both the online algorithm and the offline optimum are evaluated on the same subsampled input. We consider the canonical problems of prophet inequalities and ski-rental. In these settings, for any single subsampling rate, the classical worst-case ratios remain unchanged. We ask a stronger question: can one adversarial input remain worst-case at two distinct rates $p>q$? For prophet inequalities, in the model where the policy knows the sampling rate and learns item survival online, every instance has competitive ratio strictly below $2$ at one of the two rates, and we determine the tight simultaneous guarantee. For ski rental, in the fluid model where sampling scales the horizon, the answer depends on $q/p$. Against adversarial distributions over horizons, one unrestricted randomized algorithm achieves a strict simultaneous improvement over $e/(e-1)$ for every distribution exactly when $q/p$ is below approximately $0.34$. Requiring the algorithm to buy by the breakeven time lowers this threshold to approximately $0.31$, showing that unlike classical ski-rental algorithms, buying later can provably help in this setting. Our results therefore reveal a new form of beyond-worst-case fragility under input subsampling: instances that are worst-case at one rate need not remain hard at two rates simultaneously.

articles.title: The Golden Ratio: EF1 and Ordinal-MMS for Additive Goods
articles.summary: Every complete allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1) guarantees each of the $n$ agents her $1$-out-of-$(2n-1)$ maximin share. Can we construct allocations that satisfy EF1 together with…
articles.abstract: Every complete allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1) guarantees each of the $n$ agents her $1$-out-of-$(2n-1)$ maximin share. Can we construct allocations that satisfy EF1 together with stronger ordinal maximin share guarantees? For additive valuations, we prove that there always exists a complete allocation that is simultaneously EF1 and ($1$-out-of-$\lfloor\varphi n\rfloor$)-MMS, where $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ is the golden ratio. For bivalued valuations, where each agent may have her own two non-negative values for the goods, we obtain a complete allocation that is simultaneously envy-free up to any good (EFX) and ($1$-out-of-$\lceil(7n-1)/6\rceil$)-MMS.

articles.title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
articles.summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity,…
articles.abstract: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

articles.title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
articles.summary: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when…
articles.abstract: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.

articles.title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions
articles.summary: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free…
articles.abstract: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.

articles.title: The Price of Anarchy in Markets for Lemons
articles.summary: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can…
articles.abstract: We study the worst-case equilibrium gains from trade in simple bilateral trade mechanisms with interdependent valuations. Equilibria in such settings are typically complex, as proposed prices can convey private information held by the proposer. Such equilibria suffer lost gains from trade both due to the inefficiency introduced by screening (as in independent private value settings) and due to adverse selection. We identify broad conditions under which, nevertheless, sequential equilibria are guaranteed to achieve a constant fraction of the first-best gains from trade. Our bounds quantify the central role of rare pessimistic seller signals and rare optimistic buyer signals. The results apply to seller-proposer, buyer-proposer, and random-proposer mechanisms. The key idea in our analysis is to relate equilibrium gains from trade to proposer profits in an auxiliary market with independent private values.

articles.title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning
articles.summary: Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) aims to recover high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while preserving textual content. Existing methods treat this as a visual restoration…
articles.abstract: Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) aims to recover high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while preserving textual content. Existing methods treat this as a visual restoration problem, yet severely degraded text often cannot be read from local visual evidence alone. Humans instead read it by reasoning over image context, logical patterns, and prior knowledge. This raises a fundamental question: Does TAISR need reasoning? To answer this, we introduce two diagnostic tools. The first, ReasonText, is a human-curated benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text. The second, Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), is a recognition-based metric that measures text restoration quality without text detection errors. Evaluating twelve recent super-resolution (SR) models, we find a consistent and substantial performance drop on reasoning-required text, revealing a systematic blind spot. Two observations point to a remedy. One is that text-conditioned SR models restore text substantially better when given ground-truth text. The other is that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can read degraded text in low-resolution images through reasoning. We therefore propose Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC), a training-free plug-in that uses an external MLLM to infer the degraded text and feeds the resulting caption to a text-conditioned SR model. RTC consistently improves all six text-conditioned SR models we evaluate, especially on reasoning-required text. Surprisingly, a real-world SR model with RTC can even outperform the TAISR model with RTC, suggesting that reasoning should be a core design axis for future TAISR.

articles.title: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors
articles.summary: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization…
articles.abstract: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: https://xiliu8006.github.io/Lang-SVG/.

articles.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose
articles.summary: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic…
articles.abstract: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.

articles.title: The Noise Floor of a Quantization Comparison: Engine, restart, batch and kernel drift, measured against 8-bit and 4-bit effects in two decision models
articles.summary: A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different…
articles.abstract: A quantized model is usually judged by comparing it with its BF16 original, but that comparison changes more than the weights. It often changes the serving engine, it always runs on a different server instance, it may change how requests are batched, and on some stacks the library selects a different kernel depending only on which packages import. We measure each of these sources on the same 2,400 public decisions for two of Cloudflare's decision models, Clef-flash (9B) and Clef (27B), on an NVIDIA GB10, and state every quantization effect as the excess over them. Sources that are not quantization move between 0 and 0.92% of decisions. llama.cpp restarts are bit-identical on every record for both models. vLLM restarts flip 0, 5 and 20 decisions at BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 on Clef-flash and 4, 0 and 22 on Clef; a third instance of Clef's quantized builds (exploratory) leaves FP8 at 0 and puts NVFP4 at 4 to 22, depending on which two instances are compared. An engine change at BF16 flips 6 to 16, a batch-size change 8 to 15, and the Gated DeltaNet kernel transformers selects unasked 10 to 14. Quantization inside one engine moves more: for Clef-flash and Clef, 0.88% and 1.04% at Q8_0, 2.12% and 1.62% at FP8, 5.79% and 3.50% at Q4_K_M, and 5.79% and 5.67% at NVFP4. On both models, every 4-bit interval excludes every non-quantization source. Two of our five pre-registered predictions failed, and the same two fail when the tests are rerun on the 27B: FP8 is not inside restart noise, and changing engine moves fewer decisions than 8-bit quantization does. Accuracy hides most of this. Over the full 31,275 public questions, Clef's Q4_K_M build moves accuracy by a net six questions (-0.02 points [-0.20, +0.16]) while 436 of its decisions get worse (exploratory), and NVFP4 costs Clef-flash 0.95 points and Clef 0.65. We release the code, quantization recipes, per-record outputs and the pre-registration.

articles.title: DeNA-SGN: Deterministic Neighborhood Aggregation for Verified Spiking Graph Inference
articles.summary: Graph learning on neuromorphic substrates requires an explicit spiking realization of neighborhood aggregation, supporting control and classification. We propose DeNA-SGN, which combines fixed OR and…
articles.abstract: Graph learning on neuromorphic substrates requires an explicit spiking realization of neighborhood aggregation, supporting control and classification. We propose DeNA-SGN, which combines fixed OR and tie-inclusive Majority aggregation of binary node features with a learned signed-weight threshold classifier. A degree-dependent inhibitory construction implements Majority through shared control neurons, enabling a complete circuit compilation into SuperNeuroMAT. Across seven datasets and 41 mapped classifiers, native simulation matches the exported ANN on every evaluated class decision and output-spike pattern. On the new confirmatory Amazon Photo dataset, DeNA-SGN achieves 83.93+-0.93% current-readout accuracy and 71.61+-2.22% strict output-spike accuracy; Wiki-CS reaches 75.99+-0.54% over 20 public masks. In the matched Cora study, we achieve 74.90+-2.67% on current-readout and 68.57+-2.94% strict spike accuracy. Complete circuit and activity accounting supports analytical energy comparisons and identifies the cost of clocking inactive neurons in large deployments. Current argmax is decoded on the host, and energy is modeled rather than measured on hardware. These findings establish a reproducible route to useful graph classification with decision-matched spiking execution and explicit implementation costs.

articles.title: Galop: Billion-Scale Genetic Programming on a Single GPU
articles.summary: Genetic programming (GP) evolves populations of heterogeneous programs, whereas GPUs achieve their highest throughput when groups of threads execute the same instructions. To better align GP…
articles.abstract: Genetic programming (GP) evolves populations of heterogeneous programs, whereas GPUs achieve their highest throughput when groups of threads execute the same instructions. To better align GP evaluation with GPU execution, we present Galop, a hybrid CPU-GPU linear GP system that assigns one individual to each CUDA warp, a group of 32 threads that execute the same instructions across different fitness cases. We compare Galop against EvoGP, a recent high-performance GPU-based tree GP system, on data-rich symbolic regression across two unique GPUs, varying population size and fitness-case count. Galop completes evolutionary runs faster than EvoGP in 27 of the 28 main comparisons, with speedups of up to 13.6 times. Solution quality comparisons favour EvoGP overall, although Galop remains competitive on several problems. Galop also completes a full generation with 2.15 billion individuals on a single H100 GPU, approximately 4.0 times the largest population achieved by any other tested GP system. All five runs at this population complete 100 generations, with a median wall-clock time of 2.23 hours. These results make it practical to study GP populations in the billions on a single GPU. Galop's source code, experimental data, and reproducibility scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/xavierhillroy/Galop.

articles.title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward,…
articles.abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.

articles.title: Tailoring Optimization Approaches with Domain Knowledge in Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development
articles.summary: The paper presents an Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development (IPMD) schema, a systematic methodology for applying meta- and hyper-heuristic applications to optimization problems. In this…
articles.abstract: The paper presents an Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development (IPMD) schema, a systematic methodology for applying meta- and hyper-heuristic applications to optimization problems. In this context, we present a case study of Balancing Non-dominated Tournament Genetic Programming (BNTGP) applied to solve two NP-hard multi-objective optimization problems: routing (Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows) and scheduling (Multi-Skill Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem). The BNTGP method is based on a metaheuristic design. Its genetic programming-based representation makes BNTGP a hyper-heuristic, as it enables the exploration of a search space of heuristics for solving problems in general. The resulting heuristic can then be applied across a set of problem instances.

articles.title: Oscillatory Processing Units as a computing substrate for biomimetic intelligence
articles.summary: Biological intelligence emerges from neural activity that connects sensation, memory and action. Synaptic plasticity, neuronal assemblies and oscillations provide principles for biomimetic computing,…
articles.abstract: Biological intelligence emerges from neural activity that connects sensation, memory and action. Synaptic plasticity, neuronal assemblies and oscillations provide principles for biomimetic computing, but translating them into reusable operations requires a defined computational unit. We introduce Oscillatory Processing Units (OPUs), groups of synthetic neurons sharing a rhythm. Their directed interactions transform incoming activity and prior receiving state into an Oscillatory Occupancy Space (OOS), which becomes available to subsequent computation. We show that source--receiver conditions and oscillatory organization shape these transformations, including their geometry, persistence and historical accessibility. An Atlas of measured relationships supports prospective composition with predicted response classes. Configured circuits perform logical and numerical operations, express associative recall and generate closed-loop decisions with fixed synaptic weights. OPUs and OOS establish a computing substrate for biomimetic intelligence in which experience remains part of the state through which new input becomes action.

articles.title: A Functional Preservation Score for Auditing Connectome Operations: Compression, Alignment, Transport, and Local-Rule Writing
articles.summary: We introduce the Functional Preservation Score (FPS), a null-normalised, behaviourally grounded measure of how much of a neural network's input-output function survives a structural operation, and…
articles.abstract: We introduce the Functional Preservation Score (FPS), a null-normalised, behaviourally grounded measure of how much of a neural network's input-output function survives a structural operation, and use it to audit the operations underlying speculative "mind-migration" pipelines on public data that runs on a single laptop. Across five pre-registered studies on the C. elegans connectome, whole-brain calcium activity, and hippocampal replay, FPS yields two positive characterisations and a three-part negative. Low-bit quantisation of a real connectome exhibits a structure-dependent sparsity floor: uniform int4/ternary quantisation is forced to roughly 73%/98% effective sparsity because heavy-tailed integer synaptic weights round to zero, while mixed-precision protection of hub neurons lowers these floors to about 27%/32%. Decoded hippocampal replay sequences compress heavily yet remain identifiable at a cross-validated top-1 accuracy of 0.69 (95% CI [0.63, 0.74]; chance 0.125; permutation p < 1e-3) from latents of order 10-50 bits per event, and a bounded incremental store shows a graceful-versus-cliff capacity trade-off. The migration pipeline fails in simulation at each stage for largely independent reasons: the putative "identity payload" is not a functionally separable module (p >= 0.16 at every tested size); cross-individual functional transport via Gromov-Wasserstein collapses once the target's wiring is respected (fidelity 1.00 to 0.40, [0.31, 0.49], p < 1e-3) or alignment is imperfect (0.06, [0.00, 0.13]); and biologically plausible local plasticity cannot reach the function the target topology provably admits (gap 0.45, [0.27, 0.64], p < 1e-3, d = 2.0). We release FPS, the data loaders, and all operations as a toolkit. All results are at nematode / small-network scale and concern coherence in simulation, not the feasibility of reading or writing a living brain.

articles.title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A Constant Approximation for Consumer Surplus
articles.summary: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with submodular values generated by independent item signals. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments.
articles.abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with submodular values generated by independent item signals. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We compare two simple mechanisms. Separate selling applies money burning item by item: each item is sold in its own auction with burnt payments. Artificial-currency mechanisms give buyers personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism, which they use to bid across items. The better of our separate-selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3.80-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. For additive buyers, the factor improves to 3. The artificial-currency guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Either approach alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation bounded using separate selling.

articles.title: Second-Best Trade Is Half Efficient in Multidimensional Markets
articles.summary: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility…
articles.abstract: We prove that at least half of the first-best gains from trade can always be achieved in multidimensional two-sided markets with additive values and costs and arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints. The guarantee is achieved by a mechanism satisfying Bayesian incentive compatibility, interim individual rationality, and strong budget balance, and is tight already in single-item bilateral trade. Types are independent across agents, while the coordinates of each agent's type may be arbitrarily correlated. Feasibility constraints may couple trades across items and agents. This extends the known tight one-half guarantee for single-item bilateral trade. Our proof develops a new application of the Cai--Devanur--Weinberg duality framework. We show that the objective of every feasible dual is at least half of the first best. Strong duality then yields the guarantee without characterizing an optimal mechanism or dual. The key observation is that every feasible dual induces continuous-time Markov chains that, when stopped by exponential clocks, recover true types as expectations of virtual types. The dual constraints control the rate at which these chains change the prior distributions. We establish our bound by combining this control with a coupling of the agents' clocks.

articles.title: Adversarial risk analysis with fully probabilistic designs
articles.summary: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities,…
articles.abstract: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.

articles.title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
articles.summary: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across…
articles.abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

articles.title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
articles.summary: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a…
articles.abstract: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = ρ/ (μ_i + ρ)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $Δ_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $Ψ(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $ω^* = (4ν^2 Σ/ c')^{1/3}$, $c' = σ^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(ρ)$, and the plug-in strength $ρ^* = σ^2 / (nδ^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $ρ_{\mathrm{eff}} = ρ(e^{ζq} - 1) / (ζq)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.

articles.title: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices
articles.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on…
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference. We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/Tideway .
